subsystems.name: Chassis
subsystems.role: an inert, non-fouling body small enough to pass through capillaries (roughly 50 nm–2 µm) without being cleared immediately by the immune system.

subsystems.name: Recognition layer
subsystems.role: identifies pathogens by binding specific surface proteins or sugars.
parts: array of parallel binding sites for pattern recognition

subsystems.name: Molecular logic
subsystems.role: decides whether a detected pattern means 'pathogen' — no silicon chip works at this scale.

subsystems.name: Effector
parts: drug payload with a release trigger

subsystems.name: Power and movement
subsystems.role: supplies energy and steers the device — the hardest unsolved part.

subsystems.name: Lifecycle control
subsystems.role: lets the device be switched off, degraded or excreted after its job is done.

buildSteps.title: Build the signature library
buildSteps.detail: Catalogue surface proteins and sugars across major pathogen families, then work out how to distinguish them from human tissue — mimicry between pathogen and host proteins is the main source of autoimmune risk.

buildSteps.title: Design the scaffold
buildSteps.detail: Use DNA origami or engineered proteins that self-assemble in a test tube into a defined shape with attachment points at known positions.

buildSteps.title: Add recognition and logic
buildSteps.detail: Attach binding probes to the scaffold and wire them into a logic circuit, so the device fires only when several independent pathogen markers are present at once.

buildSteps.title: Load the effector
buildSteps.detail: Attach the killing chemistry or drug payload behind a molecular latch that only the logic circuit can open.

buildSteps.title: Validate in blood outside the body
buildSteps.detail: Run devices through flowing human blood in the lab to measure false-positive rates, clotting, fouling and off-target binding.

buildSteps.title: Test in animals
buildSteps.detail: Measure how long devices survive, where they accumulate, and whether the immune system attacks the device itself.

buildSteps.title: Scale up manufacture
buildSteps.detail: Produce self-assembling nanostructures to pharmaceutical purity, with quality control tight enough to guarantee every batch has the same shape and payload.

buildSteps.title: Clinical trials
buildSteps.detail: Test first in narrow, life-threatening infections where the risk is justified, with monitoring for immune mis-targeting.

prerequisites.why: shapes are routinely built in the lab, but made in test tubes, not inside a living body.
DNA-origami devices carrying a drug payload have been tested in animals; they are open-loop and single-use, not sensing and deciding.
strand-displacement logic works in test tubes and in cells; nothing yet computes reliably while drifting in blood.
receptor-engineered T cells already hunt specific targets in patients — proof the targeting idea works, but as cell therapy, not nanobots.
no compact, long-lived power source or steering method exists for a free-floating device in the bloodstream.
long-term fate of persistent nanoparticles in the body is poorly understood, and these devices are designed not to be cleared quickly.

pathway.milestone: nanoparticle drug carriers and receptor-engineered immune cells in the clinic
pathway.unlocks: practical delivery routes and evidence that molecular targeting works in patients.

pathway.milestone: autonomous triggered release — devices or cells that sense a biomarker and act without external command
pathway.unlocks: closed-loop therapy, first for cancer and sepsis rather than broad pathogen defence.

pathway.milestone: hybrid systems: engineered cells or gene circuits carrying out some of the intended immune functions
pathway.unlocks: most of the benefit of the concept without needing true nanomachines.

pathway.milestone: free-floating, powered, programmable devices that persist in the body
pathway.unlocks: the stated goal — but it needs breakthroughs in power, control, immunity and long-term safety that do not exist today.
